extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor lawyers, human resources professionals, worker advocates, and regulators commenting on or applying FLSA worker-classification rules
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for determining whether a worker is an `employee' or an `independent contractor' under the Fair Labor Standards Act, using the economic-reality multifactor analysis and discussion of regulatory alternatives (including the 2021 IC Rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic dependence (ultimate inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: An `employee' under the Act is an individual whom an employer suffers, permits, or otherwise employs to work . . . meant to encompass as employees all workers who, as a matter of economic reality, are economically dependent on an employer for work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focal point is whether, as a matter of economic reality, the worker is economically dependent on the business to which he renders service or is in business for himself. Economic dependence does not focus on amount of income or other income sources. (Cites: 29 CFR 795.105(b); Darden; Rutherford; Cornerstone Am.; Flint Eng'g; Superior Care.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances / economic realities test
rubrics_metrics.description: Worker classification is governed by an economic-realities test that examines the total situation rather than any single mechanical rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and the Department direct application of the multifactor totality-of-the-circumstances approach; the test is designed to capture the economic realities of the relationship between the worker and the putative employer. (Cites: Silk; Rutherford; Morrison; Dole v. Snell; Lauritzen; Selker Bros.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No single factor is dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: No one factor standing alone is dispositive; the determination does not depend on isolated factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple circuit decisions emphasize that none of the factors alone controls the outcome; the weight of each factor depends on the light it sheds on the worker's economic dependence. Apply factors flexibly based on the facts. (Cites: Silk; Parrish; Scantland; Hobbs; McFeeley; many others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (direction and supervision) factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The control factor indicates employment status if a potential employer `exercises substantial control over key aspects of the performance of the work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actual practices: a business' contractual authority to supervise or discipline may be of little relevance if in practice the business never exercises such authority. Consider the substance of control, not merely written contract rights. (Cites: 86 FR 1247; § 795.110; examples and responses to commenters.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss (including initiative/management of investment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of the individual's exercise of initiative and management of investment are both considered under this factor; the individual does not need to have an opportunity for profit or loss based on both for the factor to weigh toward independent-contractor status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the worker can realize profit or suffer loss as a result of business initiative and investment decisions. Both initiative and management of investment can be relevant, and the presence of one can be sufficient to weigh toward independent-contractor status. (Cites: 86 FR 1247 (§ 795.105(d)(1)(ii)).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment (capital investment) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Investment in facilities, equipment, or other capital is a factor in the economic-reality test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department advises that comparing the individual worker's investment to the potential employer's investment should not be part of the analysis of investment. Evaluate the worker's investment on its own terms and its bearing on economic independence. (Cites: 86 FR at 1188; 1247.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral part / extent of integration factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker's services are an integral part of the employer's business is a factor bearing on employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department discusses an `integrated unit of production' analysis and notes examples where importance to production (e.g., writing articles) is not by itself dispositive; assess how the worker's tasks fit within the employer's overall business operations. (Cites: § 795.105(c); 86 FR 1246-47; § 795.115(b)(6)(ii).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence / duration of the relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of permanence or longevity of the working relationship is a factor in the economic-reality analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer, more permanent relationships tend to indicate employee status, while temporary or project-based engagements may indicate independent-contractor status. This is one of the traditional factors courts consider. (Cites: traditional six-factor cases cited throughout.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill (professional skill and distinct occupation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The level and nature of the worker's skill and whether that skill indicates independent business status is a factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether specialized skill and professional autonomy indicate the worker is in business for himself rather than economically dependent on the employer. Consider how skill interacts with other factors (e.g., control, investment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six-factor (Silk-style) economic reality factors
rubrics_metrics.description: A traditional six-factor test (variously framed in case law) has been used to assess employment status; courts have long treated these criteria as tools to gauge economic dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a six-factor framework allows flexible application to diverse working relationships, courts caution against mechanical application; different circuits may phrase or combine factors (e.g., investment and profit/loss), but the overarching inquiry remains economic dependence. (Cites: McFeeley; Silk; cases discussing six-factor approaches.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical application; weight factors by probative value
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic-reality factors `should not be applied mechanically' and the weight of each factor depends on the facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly caution against applying any predetermined formula; consider the totality of circumstances and allow particularly probative facts to outweigh others in individual cases. (Cites: Parrish; Mr. W Fireworks; Superior Care; Saleem; Hobbs; many circuits.)

rubrics_metrics.name: List of factors is not exhaustive; consider other relevant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The list of economic reality factors is not exhaustive and any relevant evidence may be considered in determining employment status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the inquiry concerns the totality of circumstances, courts and the Department may examine various types of evidence beyond enumerated factors when they shed light on economic dependence. (Cites: Superior Care; other totality-of-circumstances authority.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractual authority versus actual exercise of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A business' contractual authority to supervise or discipline may be of little relevance if in practice the business never exercises such authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on how the relationship operates in practice rather than on formal contract terms alone; the presence of supervisory rights in a contract is not conclusive if unused. (Cites: 86 FR 1247; § 795.110.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of elevated `core' factors (policy against predetermined weighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2021 IC Rule elevated two `core' factors (control and profit/loss) and gave them near-dispositive weight if both pointed the same way; the Department finds that elevation departed from case law and introduced uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reaffirms that while some factors may be particularly important in many cases, no predetermined `core' factor should be given dispositive weight across the board; other factors may, in rare cases, outweigh those emphasized by the 2021 IC Rule. The Department seeks to provide guidance consistent with precedent rather than adopt novel, near-dispositive cores. (Cites: 86 FR 1194 et seq.; discussion rejecting 2021 IC Rule elevation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory guidance should align with case law to reduce uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking should provide detailed guidance about the application of each factor consistent with case law to decrease uncertainty about classification outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department's stated goal in this rulemaking is to reduce uncertainty by furnishing detailed, case-law-consistent guidance rather than adopting concepts that depart from precedent. The Department relies on prior appellate cautions against mechanical application and emphasizes alignment with judicial interpretations. (Cites: 86 FR 1172-75; statements about decreasing uncertainty.)
